title: The Return of the Beaver
context:
For roughly four hundred years, the beaver was missing from most of Europe. Hunters prized its dense fur, and also its castoreum, an oily secretion that was used in medicine and perfume, and by the early twentieth century only a few isolated groups survived in a handful of countries. Since the 1990s, however, a series of reintroduction projects has returned the animal to dozens of river systems, and the European population is now counted in the hundreds of thousands. Conservation bodies in several countries monitor the new colonies carefully, counting lodges each year and recording where the animals spread, because the speed of their recovery has surprised even the original supporters of the projects.

Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers, because few animals alter their surroundings so deeply. They fell trees with their teeth and use the branches, mixed with mud and stones, to build dams across streams. Behind each dam a pond forms, and the extra water spreads gradually into the neighbouring soil. Not everyone welcomes the result. Farmers have reported flooded pasture and orchards stripped of young trees, and in one Scottish valley a single dam is said to have put two hectares of grazing land under water.

Scientific monitoring, however, points to unexpected benefits. In a five-year study in the south-west of England, researchers measured the flow of a stream before and after a family of beavers settled there. The dams slowed the movement of water during storms, so that the peak of each flood was reduced by about a third, and a village downstream that had flooded regularly stayed dry. Hydrologists nevertheless warn against overstating the case. When the ground is already saturated, beaver ponds fill to the brim and can do little to hold back a major flood.

Water quality also seems to improve. The still water in a pond allows sediment to settle, and with it much of the nitrogen and phosphorus that wash off fields treated with fertiliser, so the stream below runs clearer. Wildlife responds quickly: dragonflies, frogs and wetland birds are more numerous around beaver ponds, and in dry summers trout shelter in the deeper pools. Early fears that dams would block migrating salmon have largely proved unfounded. In most conditions the fish are able to leap or swim around the obstruction, although in very low water some are delayed for several days.

The practical challenge, therefore, lies less in ecology than in human tolerance. Compensation schemes can reimburse landowners, but money does not solve every dispute, and engineers have developed cheaper alternatives. A pipe passed through a dam can keep the pond at a fixed level, while wire mesh wrapped around the trunks protects individual trees. Only when such measures fail do authorities grant licences to remove the animals. Experience in Germany and Poland, where beavers have been present for decades, suggests that coexistence is possible provided advice is offered early, before a small problem becomes a feud.

The beaver, then, is neither the villain described by its critics nor the miracle worker promised by some enthusiasts. It is a powerful animal whose effects depend on where it settles, and the sensible approach is to decide in advance which places can accommodate it and which cannot. title: The Secret of Roman Concrete
context:
The Pantheon in Rome, completed in the second century, still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its survival is remarkable when set against modern experience. Structures built with contemporary concrete often need major repairs after fifty years, and few are expected to last beyond a century. Even more puzzling are the Roman harbours, built by pouring concrete into seawater, a setting that chemists would expect to damage the material within a few decades. Yet many of these walls and piers remain standing two thousand years later.

For a long time, scholars assumed that the secret lay in the volcanic ash which Roman builders mixed with lime. The architect Vitruvius praised the ash from the region near Naples, and laboratory work confirmed that it reacts with lime and water to form a binder stronger than lime alone. This explanation, however, covers only part of the problem. It tells us why Roman concrete was good when it was new, but not why samples from harbour walls appear to have grown stronger with age.

A research team that drilled cores from an ancient harbour structure found a clue in the pores of the concrete. Crystals of two rare minerals, tobermorite and phillipsite, had grown there slowly over the centuries. Seawater seeping through the material had reacted with the volcanic ash and with the lime, and the new crystals had gradually filled spaces and sealed fine cracks. In other words, the very agent that threatens modern concrete had helped to reinforce the Roman version. The finding suggested that the ancient builders, whether by luck or experience, had created a material that responded to its environment.

A second discovery concerns the small white lumps of lime that are visible throughout Roman concrete. Archaeologists had long interpreted these lumps as signs of careless mixing. A more recent study proposes that they are intentional. According to this view, the builders mixed the ingredients while using quicklime, which is lime that has not yet been combined with water, so that the mixture became extremely hot and produced reactive lumps. When a crack later opened and water entered, the lumps dissolved and then hardened again as a mineral that filled the gap. To test the idea, researchers made concrete using the supposed Roman method and deliberately cracked it. Within two weeks, the cracks had closed, while those in a control sample made by a modern recipe remained open.

Such results should be treated with caution. Roman concrete had weaknesses that engineers cannot ignore: it set slowly, it was weak when pulled or bent, and it could not be combined with steel bars, which are essential for tall buildings and long bridges. There is also a problem of selection. The structures that have survived to the present are the ones that were well made, whereas countless Roman buildings collapsed or were demolished and left no trace. The remarkable durability of the Pantheon may therefore say more about the best builders than about the average one.

Nevertheless, the research has practical value. Cement production is responsible for roughly eight per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, so a material that repaired itself and lasted for centuries would reduce the demand for replacement. Most researchers do not propose copying the Roman recipe exactly. Instead, they hope to borrow selected features, such as the use of reactive lumps for self-repair, and adapt them for modern construction. If they succeed, the ancient builders' most useful legacy may turn out to be not their monuments, but their method.

title: How Do Birds Find Their Way?
context:
Every year, billions of birds travel thousands of kilometres between their breeding grounds and their winter homes, and many return to the very same tree or pond. How they find their way has fascinated scientists for centuries, and the answer, it turns out, is not a single instrument but a toolkit. Each tool has strengths and weaknesses, and birds appear to switch between them according to the weather, the time of day and the stage of the journey.

The first tool to be demonstrated was a sun compass. In the 1950s, a German researcher placed starlings in a circular cage with windows that let them see the sky but not the landscape. Whenever migration season came, the birds fluttered towards the same compass direction. When mirrors were used to shift the apparent position of the sun, the birds changed their direction by the same angle, proving that they were reading the sun. Since the sun moves across the sky during the day, the birds must also compensate for the time, which suggests that they possess an internal clock.

Many species travel at night, and for them the stars take over. In a classic experiment, young indigo buntings were raised inside a planetarium where the artificial sky could be controlled. The birds learned to find north by observing the point around which the stars appeared to rotate. Crucially, they did not memorise particular constellations: when the researchers made the sky rotate around a different star, the birds simply followed the new centre. Buntings that had never seen a night sky could not orient themselves at all, which shows that this ability must be learned early in life.

Birds also seem to sense the Earth's magnetic field. Robins kept in windowless rooms still hop in the direction they would normally migrate, and they become confused if the surrounding magnetic field is altered. How they detect it remains uncertain. One theory proposes that a light-sensitive protein in the eye allows birds to perceive the field as a pattern superimposed on their vision. Another suggested that tiny iron-rich particles in the beak act as a compass, but later studies found that similar particles were located in immune cells, not nerve cells, and enthusiasm for this idea has cooled.

A bird's methods change with experience. Young birds on their first journey appear to follow an inherited programme, flying in a particular direction for a particular length of time. In one study, researchers captured juvenile starlings during their autumn flight and released them hundreds of kilometres to the side. Experienced birds apparently build up a mental map using landmarks such as coastlines and mountain ranges and, according to some studies, smell. Seabirds whose sense of smell was temporarily blocked often failed to find their way back to their colonies.

The overall picture, therefore, is of redundancy rather than perfection. Birds do not rely on one sense, but weigh several cues, and when these conflict, they can recalibrate: for example, migrating thrushes use the pattern of light at sunset to adjust their magnetic compass. This flexibility has a cost when people interfere. Bright city lights can attract night migrants away from their route and cause them to circle until exhausted, which is why some cities now switch off non-essential lighting during peak migration weeks.

title: Living Food: The Science of Fermentation
context:
People have been fermenting food for at least nine thousand years. Chemical traces in pottery from northern China show that Neolithic villagers made a drink from rice, honey and fruit, and later civilisations discovered that milk, grain, fish and vegetables could all be transformed in a similar way. Their motive was probably practical rather than culinary. In a world without refrigerators, fermentation allowed a seasonal harvest to be stored for months. Many of these foods are still central to national cuisines, from yoghurt in the Balkans to kimchi in Korea.

The process is carried out by microorganisms, mostly bacteria, yeasts and moulds, which feed on sugars and release acids, alcohol or gases. Consider sauerkraut. When cabbage is shredded and mixed with salt, water is drawn out of the leaves, creating a brine. Harmful microbes struggle in this salty liquid, while lactic acid bacteria, which are already present on the leaves, multiply. As they feed they produce lactic acid, and once the acidity reaches a certain level few dangerous organisms can survive. This explains why many traditional ferments are safe, although it would be wrong to suppose that all of them are. Badly controlled fermentation of some meats and fish has caused serious poisoning.

Preservation is only part of the story. Microbes also alter flavour and nutrition. They break down proteins into amino acids, among them glutamate, which gives soy sauce, miso and aged cheese their savoury depth. Some ferments contain additional vitamins, and in cereal doughs the activity of microbes reduces phytic acid, a compound that prevents the body from absorbing minerals such as iron and zinc. Sourdough bread is sometimes said to be more nutritious than ordinary bread for this reason, though the effect depends heavily on how long the dough is left to rise.

Health claims for fermented foods are more contentious. Supporters point to probiotics, live bacteria that may benefit the gut. In one trial, volunteers who added fermented foods to their diet for ten weeks showed a greater variety of gut bacteria and lower levels of chemical markers of inflammation than a group who ate more fibre. The study was small, however, and independent scientists urge caution. Many shop-bought products are heat-treated before sale, which kills the organisms that supposedly provide the benefit, and some researchers suspect that the compounds produced during fermentation, rather than the living microbes, may be responsible for any improvement.

A different debate concerns the way fermentation is done. Large manufacturers use carefully selected starter cultures to guarantee speed, safety and a consistent taste. Artisans reply that relying on wild microbes gives richer, more varied flavours. It is often assumed that those microbes come from the region, so that bread from one city will always taste different from bread from another. A worldwide survey of sourdough starters, however, found that geography explained very little. Factors such as the type of flour and the hands of the baker proved to be more important.

Whatever the truth of the individual claims, interest in fermentation shows no sign of fading. Home cooks fill jars with cabbage and carrots, and restaurants list their own house-made vinegars. The enthusiasm is understandable, since few cooking techniques are so cheap or so rewarding. Yet a little scepticism is healthy. Fermentation is a craft with a long history, not a miracle cure, and the evidence for its benefits should be judged by the same standards as any other medical claim.

title: The Public Library: A Changing Institution
context:
The idea of collecting writing in one place is very old, but the earliest libraries were not for the public. The palace library at Nineveh, assembled by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in the seventh century BCE, held tens of thousands of clay tablets, and the famous library at Alexandria sought to gather the knowledge of the known world. Both were royal projects, designed to display power as much as to preserve learning, and access was restricted to scribes and scholars. An ordinary citizen would not have been admitted.

The notion that ordinary people might borrow books developed much later. In the eighteenth century, groups of readers began to form subscription libraries, in which members paid a fee to share a collection. Benjamin Franklin helped to found one in Philadelphia in 1731. Subscription libraries, however, excluded those who could not afford the fee, and the decisive step was to fund libraries from taxation. Britain passed a law in 1850 allowing towns to raise a small local tax for this purpose, and Boston opened a free library for its citizens soon afterwards. Supporters argued that access to books would improve the working classes and, as one reformer put it, draw them away from the public house.

Philanthropy accelerated the movement. Between 1883 and 1929 the steel magnate Andrew Carnegie paid for the construction of over two thousand five hundred libraries around the English-speaking world. He attached a condition: the town had to provide the land and commit public money to the running costs. Carnegie regarded libraries as a ladder for those who wished to educate themselves, since he had used one himself as a boy. Critics, then and now, have questioned whether gifts from a man who had made his fortune in an industry known for harsh working conditions could be welcomed without reservation, and some towns found the maintenance burden heavier than they had expected.

The twentieth century transformed the experience of using a library. Early public libraries kept books in closed stacks, and readers had to ask a clerk to fetch them. The introduction of open shelves, where visitors could browse and choose for themselves, was resisted by many librarians, who feared that books would be stolen. Experience proved otherwise, and borrowing rose sharply. Dedicated children's rooms followed, along with trained staff who could recommend books, and by the middle of the century the library had become a familiar part of town life.

The arrival of the internet led many commentators to predict the death of the library. That has not happened. Visits have fallen in some countries, but remain high in others, and libraries have responded by lending e-books and offering free computers. Many have also taken on tasks that have little to do with books. Staff help unemployed people to write job applications, run language classes for immigrants, and provide a warm, quiet place for those who have nowhere else to go. Not all communities have been able to keep up: in England, hundreds of branches have closed since 2010 as councils have tried to reduce their spending.

This history suggests that the value of a library cannot be calculated simply by counting loans. A library is a form of what sociologists call social infrastructure, a shared space that brings different people together at little cost. Such places are easy to overlook when budgets are discussed, because their benefits are spread widely and appear slowly. Yet once they have gone, they are very difficult to replace.

title: Bleached Reefs and the Search for Resilience
context:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to about a quarter of all marine species. The builders of a reef are corals, which are animals, not plants. Each is a colony of tiny polyps whose tissues contain microscopic algae. The two live in partnership: the algae use sunlight to make sugars, supplying the coral with most of its energy, while the coral provides shelter and the chemicals the algae need. The arrangement is highly efficient, but it is also delicate. Their loss would therefore affect fisheries and coastal communities as well as divers and scientists.

Trouble begins when the water stays about one degree Celsius above the normal summer maximum for several weeks. Under heat stress, the algae start to produce harmful compounds, and the coral responds by expelling them. Without the algae, the coral's transparent tissue reveals the white skeleton beneath, hence the term bleaching. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead. If temperatures fall within a few weeks, the algae can return and the colony recovers. If the heat continues, however, the coral starves. The first worldwide bleaching event was recorded in 1998, and since then such events have become more frequent. On the Great Barrier Reef, the average gap between severe episodes has shrunk from decades to roughly six years, and in 2016 and 2017 the reef was struck twice in succession, leaving too little time for recovery.

Yet the damage has not been uniform. Fast-growing branching corals, which provide hiding places for fish, are among the most vulnerable, whereas slow-growing boulder-shaped species often survive. Some reefs have even adapted to extraordinary conditions: those in the Persian Gulf endure summer temperatures that would kill most corals elsewhere. These exceptions have encouraged scientists to ask whether resilience can be encouraged, or even engineered.

Several approaches are being tested. In selective breeding, researchers cross the most heat-tolerant colonies and raise their offspring in tanks, hoping to produce tougher stock. Others try exposing young corals to mild stress so that they become accustomed to it, or replacing their algae with heat-tolerant varieties. In coral gardening, fragments are grown in underwater nurseries and then attached to damaged reefs. These projects have produced encouraging results on a small scale, but a nursery that grows thousands of fragments a year is dwarfed by a reef system stretching over two thousand kilometres. Critics add that favouring a few tolerant strains may reduce genetic diversity, leaving reefs vulnerable to other threats.

Local conditions also matter. Reefs that suffer from polluted run-off or from overfishing recover more slowly than those that do not. In particular, parrotfish and other grazing species keep seaweed under control, and when they are caught in excess, seaweed can smother the young corals trying to re-establish themselves. Protecting reefs from these local pressures therefore buys valuable time, and in several regions it has measurably improved survival rates after bleaching.

Time, though, is what the technology cannot ultimately provide. Climate models suggest that at 1.5 degrees of global warming, between seventy and ninety per cent of warm-water reefs would be lost, and at two degrees virtually all of them. Interventions such as breeding and gardening are best seen as emergency measures that give reefs a chance to survive until emissions fall. They are worth pursuing, but they are not a substitute for the harder task of cutting those emissions.

title: From Shells to Screens: A Short History of Money
context:
Most of us were taught that money grew out of barter. According to this familiar story, early people swapped goods directly, and when this proved clumsy, since a shoemaker with a surplus of shoes might not find a baker who needed them, they began to use a common item such as shells or metal as a go-between. The tale is appealing, but anthropologists have found little evidence for it. No society has been discovered that depended mainly on barter between its own members. Instead, small communities typically relied on gifts, favours and informal credit, remembering who owed what to whom.

The earliest written records support this view. Around 3000 BCE, temple officials in Mesopotamia used clay tablets to record debts, mostly in barley, and fixed their value against a standard weight of silver. The silver itself rarely changed hands. It served as a unit of account, a way of comparing the worth of different goods, rather than as a means of payment. In other words, the idea of a measure of value seems to have preceded the invention of any physical currency.

Coins arrived much later. The kingdom of Lydia, in what is now Turkey, produced stamped lumps of a natural gold-and-silver alloy in the seventh century BCE. The stamp was the important feature. By guaranteeing weight and purity, the ruler spared buyers and sellers from having to weigh and test the metal at every transaction. Coins proved especially useful for paying armies, and the practice spread quickly across the Greek world. China developed its own tradition independently, casting bronze coins with a hole in the middle so that they could be strung together in bundles.

Heavy coins are inconvenient for large payments, which led to another innovation. In China, from about the ninth century CE, merchants began to leave their coins with trusted deposit shops in exchange for paper receipts that could be redeemed elsewhere. In the eleventh century the government took over the issue of paper notes. The result was a success until officials found that they could solve their financial problems by printing more, which caused prices to rise. Europe adopted paper money many centuries later, when goldsmiths and early banks began to issue notes promising to pay the bearer in precious metal on demand.

For a long time, a note's value was linked to a store of gold. The last connection was cut in 1971, when the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold. Today most national currencies are fiat money, which has no intrinsic worth. It is valuable because the government declares it legal tender and agrees to accept it as payment for taxes, and above all because people expect others to accept it too. Money, in other words, works only as long as it is trusted.

That trust now attaches increasingly to numbers rather than objects. The majority of money exists only as entries in bank databases. In Kenya, a mobile phone service allows people with no bank account to send payments by text message, and it has become an important part of the economy. Cryptocurrencies, designed to function without any central authority, represent a more radical experiment, though their prices have fluctuated so wildly that few people use them for everyday purchases. Whatever form it takes, money is best understood not as a thing but as a shared belief, one which societies have found many ingenious ways to record.

title: Clutter in Orbit
context:
Since the launch of Sputnik in 1957, humanity has sent many thousands of satellites into orbit, but only a minority are still working. The rest have joined an expanding cloud of debris that includes spent rocket stages, dead satellites and fragments produced by explosions and collisions. Space agencies track about thirty thousand objects larger than a cricket ball, and statistical models estimate that there are more than a hundred million pieces bigger than a millimetre. Size is misleading, because everything in orbit moves at around seven kilometres per second. At that speed, a fleck of paint can chip a spacecraft window and a bolt can destroy a satellite.

In 1978, the American scientist Donald Kessler proposed that the debris problem could eventually feed on itself. A collision creates fragments, which in turn cause further collisions, until certain orbits become unusable for generations. Fortunately, this chain reaction has not yet occurred, but two events showed how real the danger is. In 2007, a Chinese test destroyed an old weather satellite with a missile, scattering thousands of tracked fragments. Two years later, an American communications satellite and a defunct Russian one collided by accident, the first such collision between two intact satellites. Some altitudes, notably around 800 kilometres, are now thought to be dangerously crowded.

More recently, attention has turned to mega-constellations, networks of thousands of small satellites offering internet access. Their orbits are low, at around 550 kilometres, where the thin upper atmosphere drags dead satellites down within a few years, so the long-term debris risk is smaller than at higher altitudes. Nevertheless, the sheer number of satellites raises the chance of collisions, and astronomers complain that bright trails across the sky are spoiling their images. Operators promise to bring satellites down at the end of their lives, but critics note that a noticeable number have failed soon after launch, and a failed satellite cannot steer itself out of the way.

Avoiding collisions depends on tracking. Radars and telescopes on the ground monitor objects of about ten centimetres and larger, and when a close approach is predicted, the operator may move its satellite out of the way. The International Space Station has done so dozens of times. Such manoeuvres consume fuel and interrupt normal operations, and because the predicted positions of debris are uncertain, many are carried out for encounters that would not actually have led to a collision. Objects too small to be tracked but large enough to cause damage cannot be avoided at all.

Several methods of removal have been suggested, including nets, harpoons, robotic arms and magnets attached to special docking plates. In 2018, a small demonstration mission successfully captured a test target with a net. However, such methods are costly, and the cost of removing a single large object may approach the cost of building a new satellite. There are legal obstacles as well. Under international treaty, a country retains ownership of anything it launches even when it is dead, which means that nobody may remove it without permission.

For these reasons, many experts believe that the priority should be prevention. Existing guidelines advise that satellites be moved out of crowded orbits when their missions end, and that leftover fuel be released so that old rocket stages cannot explode. Compliance, though, is voluntary and uneven. Some economists propose that operators should pay a fee for the right to use busy orbits, which would reward those who keep them clean. Cleaning up is possible in principle, but it is cheaper, and far more effective, not to make the mess in the first place.

title: The Art of Remembering
context:
According to an ancient legend, the Greek poet Simonides was giving a speech at a banquet when he was called outside. While he was away, the roof of the hall collapsed, crushing the guests so badly that their relatives could not recognise them. Simonides, however, could name every victim, because he remembered where each had been sitting. The story may be invented, but it is said to have inspired the method of loci, a technique later used by Roman orators who needed to deliver long speeches without notes.

The method is simple. You select a place you know well, such as your home, and picture a route through it. Along the route, you place vivid images representing the things you want to remember: to recall a shopping list, you might imagine a giant loaf of bread blocking the front door and a goose sitting in the sink. To retrieve the list, you walk through the building in your mind and see what you find. Practitioners often compare the process to hanging coats on pegs in a hallway that they already know by heart. The technique works for two reasons. Human brains evolved to remember places, so locations provide a strong framework. And unusual, exaggerated images are easier to recall than abstract words.

Modern research has taken these claims seriously. Scientists studied people who compete in memory championships and found, perhaps surprisingly, that their brains were structurally normal and their intelligence scores were no higher than average. What distinguished them was that, when they memorised, regions linked with spatial memory became unusually active. Does that mean anyone can learn the skill? An experiment suggests so. Volunteers with ordinary memories trained for about forty minutes a day over six weeks, and the average number of words they could recall from a list of seventy-two rose from around twenty-six to around sixty-two, an improvement that was still visible four months later.

The method has limits, though. It is excellent for lists and sequences, such as the order of the planets or the items of a speech, but it does nothing to help a student understand why a historical event happened or how an equation works. Some educators therefore dismiss memorisation as an outdated habit. Others reply that facts stored in the mind are the raw material of creative thought, and that a person who must look everything up cannot easily make connections. Learning the technique also demands effort, since each route must be prepared and rehearsed, and using the same route again and again can lead to confusion between old and new images.

Two other strategies are supported by strong evidence. The first is spaced repetition. In the 1880s, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised long lists of nonsense syllables and discovered that forgetting is fastest soon after learning. Reviewing the material at increasing intervals, he found, flattens this curve, and many modern apps are built around the idea. The second is retrieval practice. Students who tested themselves on a text remembered more a week later than those who simply read it again, even though the re-readers felt more confident.

The methods are therefore best seen as complements rather than rivals. A memory palace gives structure to facts that must be learned in order; spacing and self-testing help them last. None of them replaces understanding, but a mind that is trained to hold information reliably has more room to think about what that information means.

title: Cities That Soak Up the Rain
context:
For more than a century, cities dealt with rain by getting rid of it as fast as possible. Roofs, roads and car parks were laid with hard materials, and a network of underground pipes carried the runoff to the nearest river. The system works adequately in ordinary weather, but it is easily overwhelmed by the intense downpours that climate change is making more common. When the pipes fill, water backs up and floods streets, basements and underground railways. In 2016, severe flooding killed dozens of people in the Chinese city of Wuhan, which had been chosen the year before as one of the first pilot cities for a national policy known as the sponge city, under which urban areas are expected to absorb and reuse most of their rainfall.

The principle is to slow, store and soak up water where it falls, rather than rush it away. Planners achieve this by replacing solid paving with permeable surfaces through which water drains into the ground, by planting gardens that are deliberately lower than the surrounding pavement so that rain collects in them, and by covering roofs with vegetation that holds moisture. Larger projects restore wetlands or build ponds that remain empty in dry weather but fill during storms. In Copenhagen, after a cloudburst in 2011 caused damage worth about a billion euros, the authorities began redesigning streets so that during extreme rain they act as channels, guiding water towards parks and the harbour.

The attraction of this approach is that it delivers more than flood protection. Vegetation cools the air in summer, and soil filters oil and other pollutants from road water before it reaches rivers. Water that sinks into the ground replenishes underground reserves, a valuable gain in regions facing shortages. Parks and gardens also make neighbourhoods pleasanter, and property prices near them tend to rise. When Philadelphia compared the cost of enlarging its sewers with the cost of green measures, officials concluded that the latter would be cheaper and bring additional benefits.

Nevertheless, sponge cities are not a universal cure. Soil that is rich in clay absorbs water slowly, and in places where the groundwater is already close to the surface there is nowhere for rain to go. Maintenance is another problem: permeable paving clogs with dirt, and rain gardens need regular weeding, yet budgets for upkeep are often neglected once a project has been opened with fanfare. A review of the first Chinese pilot cities found that some had spent large sums and still suffered floods, partly because the schemes were designed for ordinary storms rather than extreme ones.

Practical and political obstacles also arise. In dense old districts there is little space, and retrofitting is expensive and disruptive, so new developments are generally easier to adapt than established ones. Responsibility is frequently divided among departments for roads, water and parks, each with its own priorities. Some governments have found that financial incentives help. In Germany, many municipalities charge property owners a separate fee based on the area of hard surface on their land, which encourages owners to install green roofs or permeable paving.

The sensible conclusion is that the sponge should supplement the pipe, not replace it. Where conditions are suitable, absorbing water at its source reduces pressure on the drainage network and brings other advantages. But it requires patient maintenance and honest assessment of what each site can handle. Cities that treat the idea as a fashionable label, rather than as a long-term commitment, are likely to be disappointed.
